Deeper
dēp'-ēr
adj. (comparative of deep: further in, further down, harder to reach or to know)
Comparative of deep, Saxon deop. Its two great uses in the Authorized Version are diagnostic and doxological: the priest looking to see whether a plague is deeper than the skin, and Zophar asking what a man can know of a wisdom deeper than hell.

Biblical Definition

The most frequent use of deeper in Scripture belongs to the leprosy law, where it is a diagnostic word: “when the hair in the plague is turned white, and the plague in sight be deeper than the skin of his flesh, it is a plague of leprosy” (Lev 13:3). The priest is trained to ask one question — is this on the surface, or has it gone in? A blemish that lies upon the skin may pass; a plague that lies beneath it defiles. Scripture uses that trained eye everywhere afterward. Sin that has gone in is not managed by scrubbing the surface, and a religion that treats it as surface work is precisely what the prophets and our Lord condemn. The second use lifts the same word to God: “It is as high as heaven; what canst thou do? deeper than hell; what canst thou know?” (Job 11:8). Zophar is a poor comforter, but the sentence is true — the searching out of God is deeper than a creature's line will reach. And Isaiah uses it of judgment by an incomprehensible tongue: “a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive” (Isa 33:19), the Assyrian whose words could not be understood, promised to be seen no more. Three depths, then: the depth of the disease, the depth of God, and the depth of a judgment that speaks in a language you cannot answer.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines deep as extending far below the surface, descending far downward, and figuratively as profound, not easily fathomed.

expand to see more

DEEP, a. Extending or being far below the surface; descending far downward; profound; opposed to shallow.

1. Low in situation; being or descending far below the adjacent land.

2. Not superficial or obvious; hidden; secret; as the deep things of God.

3. Sagacious; penetrating; having the power to enter far into a subject; as a deep divine.

Key Scripture

Lev 13:3 — "And the priest shall look on the plague in the skin of the flesh: and when the hair in the plague is turned white, and the plague in sight be deeper than the skin of his flesh, it is a plague of leprosy: and the priest shall look on him, and pronounce him unclean."

Job 11:8 — "It is as high as heaven; what canst thou do? deeper than hell; what canst thou know?"

Lev 13:31 — "And if the priest look on the plague of the scall, and, behold, it be not in sight deeper than the skin, and that there is no black hair in it; then the priest shall shut up him that hath the plague of the scall seven days:"

Isa 33:19 — "Thou shalt not see a fierce people, a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive; of a stammering tongue, that thou canst not understand."

Modern Corruption

“Deeper” has become a compliment for the vague; in Scripture it is a word for what is verified, not for what is merely obscure.

expand to see more

Contemporary religious speech uses deeper as a term of approval for teaching that is hard to pin down — a deeper truth, a deeper meaning, a deeper reading — where the depth claimed is usually only distance from the text. The priest of Leviticus 13 shows what biblical depth-language actually does: it is a test with a determinate answer, applied by an appointed man, in the light, with a rule. Depth in Scripture is examined, not asserted. The teacher who says his sense is deeper and cannot show it in the words has said nothing.

The genuine depth is the one Zophar names and Paul takes up: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God (Rom 11:33). It is not a hidden meaning behind the text but the inexhaustible God whom the plain text truly reveals. The right response to it is worship and a closed mouth, not a claim to have sounded it. What is deeper than hell no man can know; what God has written He has written to be understood.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'amoq (H6013), deep, unsearchable; 'amaq (H6009), to be deep, to make deep; Greek bathos (G899), depth.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'amoq (H6013) — deep, mysterious; Leviticus 13 of the plague deeper than the skin, Isaiah 33:19 of a deeper speech.

Hebrew 'amaq (H6009) — to be deep; Job 11:8, deeper than hell (Sheol).

Hebrew she'owl (H7585) — the grave, the unseen state of the dead; the measure of depth in Job's comparison.

Greek bathos (G899) — depth; Romans 11:33 (the depth of the riches of the wisdom of God), 1 Corinthians 2:10 (the deep things of God).

Greek bathuno (G900) — to deepen, to dig deep; Luke 6:48, of the house founded upon a rock.

Usage

"“Deeper than the skin” — the priest's one question about every plague."

"“Deeper than hell; what canst thou know?” — and Zophar was right about that much."

"“A deeper speech than thou canst perceive” — judgment in a tongue you cannot answer."
